concept.overview: Ansible is an open-source automation tool for configuration management, application deployment, and orchestration. You describe the desired state of your servers in YAML playbooks, and Ansible connects over SSH (no agent required) to make each host match that state. Because tasks are idempotent, running a playbook repeatedly converges every machine to the same configuration without causing drift or duplicate changes.
concept.whyItMatters: Configuring servers by hand does not scale and cannot be reviewed or reproduced. Ansible turns configuration into version-controlled code that runs identically across one host or a thousand. Its agentless SSH model and readable YAML make it one of the easiest automation tools to adopt, and it is a staple of DevOps interviews and real infrastructure.
useCases: Provisioning and configuring servers consistently (packages, users, services)
Deploying applications and rolling out updates across fleets
Enforcing a known-good state and remediating configuration drift
Orchestrating multi-tier rollouts with ordering and handlers
Ad-hoc operational tasks across many hosts (patching, restarts)
concept.architecture: Ansible runs from a control node — your laptop or a CI runner — and manages inventory hosts with no agent installed on them. The inventory lists hosts and groups (static INI/YAML or dynamic from a cloud). A playbook is an ordered list of plays; each play targets a host group and runs tasks, where each task invokes a module (e.g., apt, copy, service) that does the actual work idempotently. Ansible gathers facts (system data) about each host, connects over SSH (or WinRM), and executes modules by pushing small programs, running them, and removing them. Roles package reusable tasks, templates, and variables; handlers run only when notified (e.g., restart a service after its config changes). Ansible Vault encrypts secrets in the repo.

definitions.def: The machine that runs Ansible and connects out to managed hosts.
The list of managed hosts and groups, static or dynamically generated.
A YAML file of plays and tasks describing the desired state.
A unit of work Ansible executes (apt, copy, service, etc.), designed to be idempotent.
A reusable, structured bundle of tasks, templates, handlers, and variables.
A task that runs only when notified by another task (e.g., restart on config change).
System information Ansible gathers about each host before running tasks.

commands.desc: Ad-hoc check that hosts are reachable.
Run a playbook against the inventory.
Dry run: report changes without applying (check mode).
Restrict a run to a host group.
Run only tasks with a given tag.
Show file changes as they are applied.

bestPractices: Design tasks to be idempotent; prefer modules over raw shell/command.
Organize reusable configuration into roles with clear variables and defaults.
Encrypt secrets with Ansible Vault; never commit plaintext credentials.
Use --check (and --diff) to preview changes before applying to production.
Keep inventories and group_vars in version control alongside playbooks.
pitfalls: Overusing the shell/command modules, breaking idempotency and check mode.
Hardcoding secrets in playbooks instead of using Vault.
No inventory grouping, so you can't target subsets safely.
Ignoring handler notifications, so services don't restart after config changes.
Running against 'all' by mistake and changing every host at once.
cheatSheet: Notify + handler: task 'notify: restart nginx' → handler restarts it

quiz.question: Ansible is agentless and connects to managed hosts over SSH.
quiz.explanation: No agent is installed on hosts; Ansible pushes modules over SSH (or WinRM).

quiz.question: What language are Ansible playbooks written in?
quiz.explanation: Playbooks are YAML files describing plays and tasks.

quiz.question: What does 'idempotent' mean for an Ansible task?
options: Re-running it converges to the same state without duplicate changes
quiz.explanation: Idempotent tasks make a change only if needed, so repeated runs are safe.

quiz.question: What is an Ansible role?
options: A reusable bundle of tasks, templates, handlers, and variables
quiz.explanation: Roles package reusable configuration for use across playbooks and projects.

quiz.question: Which flag previews changes without applying them?
quiz.explanation: --check is dry-run/check mode; pair with --diff to see file changes.

quiz.question: Ansible Vault encrypts sensitive data so it can live safely in version control.
quiz.explanation: Vault encrypts files/variables so secrets aren't stored in plaintext.

quiz.question: What triggers a handler to run?
quiz.explanation: Handlers run only when a task notifies them, typically at the end of a play.

quiz.question: You want to restart nginx only when its config file changes. Best approach?
options: Use a handler notified by the config task
quiz.explanation: A handler notified on config change restarts the service only when needed, preserving idempotency.

quiz.question: What does the inventory define?
quiz.explanation: Inventory lists hosts and groups Ansible manages.

quiz.question: Why prefer the 'service' module over 'shell: systemctl restart'?
options: It's idempotent and works with check mode
quiz.explanation: Purpose-built modules are idempotent and report changes correctly; raw shell is not.

tasks.title: Ping an inventory
steps: Create an inventory listing one or more hosts
Set up SSH access to them
successCriteria: All hosts respond to the ping module

tasks.title: Write a configuration playbook
tasks.goal: Install and configure a service declaratively.
steps: Write a playbook that installs nginx via the package module
Template the config with the template module
Add a handler to restart nginx on config change
successCriteria: The handler restarts nginx only when the config changes

tasks.title: Refactor into a role with Vault
steps: Store a secret in an Ansible Vault file
Reference the encrypted variable from the role
Run the playbook using the vault password
successCriteria: The role is reused across host groups
No plaintext secrets exist in the repo

tasks.title: Rolling multi-tier deployment
steps: Define web and db groups in inventory
Use serial to update web hosts in batches
Order plays so the database is configured first
Verify zero-downtime by checking health between batches
successCriteria: Web hosts update in controlled batches
The service stays available throughout the rollout
